```{r setup, include = FALSE}
                      dpi = 72, out.width = "100%")
```

```{r, eval = !has_cub, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("**This vignette needs the 'CUB' package (for the `univer` data), which is not installed: code is shown but not run.**")
```

**DistrViz** draws *distributional data tables*: tables where each cell
(a statistical unit, i.e. a row, observed on a variable, i.e. a column) is a
whole distribution rather than a single number. Two kinds of tables are
supported:

* matrices of **histograms**, the `MatH` objects of the **HistDAWass**
  package (continuous variables);
* matrices of **discrete distributions**, the `MatD` objects of the
  **DDAWASS** package (e.g. ratings on a Likert scale, counts).

All the plotting functions (`gei_plot()`, `gei_grid()`, `dist_heatmap()`)
accept these objects directly, as well as raw data frames, but they all work
on a common intermediate object, built by `dv_data()`. This vignette explains
how `dv_data()` maps the distributions to colours; the next two vignettes
present the Green Eyes plots and the distributional heatmaps.

```{r}
library(DistrViz)
library(DDAWASS)
```

## The data

We use the same data of the **DDAWASS** vignettes: the `univer` survey of the
**CUB** package, where 2179 students of the University of Naples Federico II
rated on a 1-7 scale (1 = extremely unsatisfied, 7 = extremely satisfied) five
aspects of the orientation services: the information received (`informat`),
the willingness of the staff (`willingn`), the office hours (`officeho`), the
competence of the staff (`compete`) and the global satisfaction (`global`).

```{r}
data(univer, package = "CUB")
univer$Faculty <- factor(sprintf("F%02d", univer$faculty))
univer$Gender  <- factor(univer$gender, levels = 0:1, labels = c("M", "W"))
items <- c("informat", "willingn", "officeho", "compete", "global")
```

The statistical units are the groups of students defined by faculty and
gender: each of the 26 groups is described by the five distributions of the
ratings given by its members.

```{r}
M <- data2MatD(univer, unit = c("Faculty", "Gender"), vars = items,
               support = 1:7, min.n = 10)
M
```

## Building a `dvdata` object

`dv_data()` turns the table into a long data frame with one row for each
support value of each cell, together with its probability (`freq`), the
cumulative distribution function before and after the value (`cdf_lo`,
`cdf`) and a **colour position** `u` in $[0, 1]$.

```{r}
dv <- dv_data(M, ranges = c(1, 7))
dv
```

The same object can be built directly from the microdata: the grouping
columns go in `unit`, the items in `vars`, and `support` and `min.n` are
passed to `DDAWASS::data2MatD()`. When `support` is given, its range is used
as the colour range.

```{r}
dv2 <- dv_data(univer, unit = c("Faculty", "Gender"), vars = items,
               support = 1:7, min.n = 10)
all.equal(dv$df$u, dv2$df$u)
```

A table of frequencies in long format (one row for each unit, variable and
value) is read when the `freq` column is given:

```{r}
tab <- as.data.frame(table(unit = univer$Faculty, value = univer$global))
tab$variable <- "global"
head(tab)
dv_global <- dv_data(tab, unit = "unit", value = "value", freq = "Freq",
                     ranges = c(1, 7))
dv_global
```

## How values become colours

### Discrete distributions

For a `MatD`, a value $x$ of variable $j$ gets the position
$$u = \frac{x - a_j}{b_j - a_j},$$
where $[a_j, b_j]$ is the range of the variable. With `ranges = c(1, 7)` the
range is the admissible range of the rating scale, so that the colour of a
rating does not depend on the data: a 1 is always dark red, a 7 is always
dark green. Without `ranges`, the observed range of each variable is used.

When the variables are measured on **different scales** (e.g. a 0-10 scale and
a 1-5 scale, as in many surveys), `ranges` can be a two-column matrix with one
row per variable, so that the ends of each scale get the same colours:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
dv_data(M, ranges = cbind(min = c(0, 1, 1, 1), max = c(10, 5, 4, 2)))
```

Two other schemes are available:

* `scheme = "global"`: the same (observed) range for all the variables;
* `scheme = "standardized"`: each variable is standardized with its
  Wasserstein mean and standard deviation, and the colours span $\pm 3$
  standard deviations around the mean. This is useful to compare variables
  measured on completely different scales.

### Histograms

A `MatH` is first discretized: the range of each variable is split into
`n_levels` equal-width classes and each histogram is turned into the discrete
distribution of the probabilities of the classes (see
`DDAWASS::MatH2MatD()`). The $k$-th class gets the position
$u = (k-1)/(n_\text{levels}-1)$. The classes span the observed range of each
variable, or the range given in `ranges` (see the fourth vignette). The tooltips of the interactive plots report
the class bounds.

```{r}
dvh <- dv_data(HistDAWass::BLOOD, n_levels = 12)
dvh
```

## Palettes

The positions `u` are mapped to colours by a continuous palette. The default,
`"Paquin"`, goes from dark red (low values) to dark green (high values): it is
the palette of the Green Eyes plots. `dv_palette()` also offers `"Hiroshige"`,
`"Grey"` and all the palettes of `grDevices::hcl.pals()`; a vector of colours
can be used as well.

```{r, fig.height = 2.6}
show_pal <- function(pals, n = 64) {
  op <- par(mar = c(0.5, 7, 0.5, 0.5))
  on.exit(par(op))
  plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0.5, length(pals) + 0.5), axes = FALSE,
       xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_along(pals)) {
    cl <- dv_palette(pals[i], n)
    rect((seq_len(n) - 1) / n, i - 0.4, seq_len(n) / n, i + 0.4, col = cl, border = NA)
  }
  axis(2, at = seq_along(pals), labels = pals, las = 1, tick = FALSE)
}
show_pal(c("Paquin", "Hiroshige", "RdYlGn", "Zissou 1", "Blue-Red 3", "Viridis"))
```

All the plotting functions have a `palette` and a `reverse` argument.
